【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【47】**Elderly nonhypertensive patients with superficial lobar hemorrhages should be suspected of having congophilic angiopathy. These hemorrhages are often recurrent which can be demonstrated by gradient ECHO MRI (demonstrates hemosiderin from prior bleeds).**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【47】**Elderly nonhypertensive patients with superficial lobar hemorrhages should be suspected of having congophilic angiopathy. These hemorrhages are often recurrent which can be demonstrated by gradient ECHO MRI (demonstrates hemosiderin from prior bleeds).**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【49】**Venous thrombosis with hemorrhage should be suspected in pregnant patients and those in a hypercoagulable state. Pre-ceding sense headache lethargy and seizures are common.**

【50】**Vasculopathy or vasculitis may also cause nonhyperten-sive hemorrhage.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【47】**Elderly nonhypertensive patients with superficial lobar hemorrhages should be suspected of having congophilic angiopathy. These hemorrhages are often recurrent which can be demonstrated by gradient ECHO MRI (demonstrates hemosiderin from prior bleeds).**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【49】**Venous thrombosis with hemorrhage should be suspected in pregnant patients and those in a hypercoagulable state. Pre-ceding sense headache lethargy and seizures are common.**

【50】**Vasculopathy or vasculitis may also cause nonhyperten-sive hemorrhage.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【47】**Elderly nonhypertensive patients with superficial lobar hemorrhages should be suspected of having congophilic angiopathy. These hemorrhages are often recurrent which can be demonstrated by gradient ECHO MRI (demonstrates hemosiderin from prior bleeds).**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【42】**Non-Hypertensive Causes of Parenchymal and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【43】**There are multiple causes of parenchymal and subarachnoid hemorrhage that are not caused by idiopathic hypertension. Many are caused by induced hypertension in patients with un-derlying cystic aneurysms and vascular malformations. They frequently have very specific clinical profiles that are diag-nostic.**

【44】**Idiopathic perimesencephalic hemorrhage may account for approximately 10% of all SAH. It rarely occurs with con-genital aneurysms and seems more likely to be caused by leakage of blood from the prepontine venous plexus. Most patients have no focal neurologic deficits on admission. The headache associated with this bleed reaches maximum inten-sity within minutes rather than seconds. There is no loss of consciousness with the ictus and no rebleeding or delayed is-chemia.**

【45】**Mycolic aneurysm most often occur in the distal branches of the MCA and cause both intraparenchymal and SAH. They may be the initial presentation of SBE.**

【46】**Drug abuse with sympathomimetic agents and cocaine in-duce hypertension and cause hemorrhage as well as ischemic stroke. Cocaine in particular is associated with approximately20% of ICHfrom an underlying aneurysm or vascular malfor-mation. Drug abuse and SBE are coextensive.**

【47】**Elderly nonhypertensive patients with superficial lobar hemorrhages should be suspected of having congophilic angiopathy. These hemorrhages are often recurrent which can be demonstrated by gradient ECHO MRI (demonstrates hemosiderin from prior bleeds).**

【48】**Traumatic intracranial hemorrhage frequently are delayed to 4-7 days after ictus. They occur in the originally damaged brain issue.**

【49】**Venous thrombosis with hemorrhage should be suspected in pregnant patients and those in a hypercoagulable state. Pre-ceding sense headache lethargy and seizures are common.**

【50】**Vasculopathy or vasculitis may also cause nonhyperten-sive hemorrhage.**

【200】**Subarachnoid Hemorrhage**

【201】**Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a devastating neurologic illness that carries a mortality of 30% with each bleed and very sig-nificant mortality in survivors.**

【202】**The ictus is frequently characteristic as patients suffer a severe headache that reaches maximum intensity instantly. The headache is frequently basioccipital and then shifts to frontal areas. It is associated with vomiting in a significant number of patients with attendant loss of consciousness in ap-proximately 30-50%. The neck is stiff， patients have positive Kearnig's and Brudzinski's signs and focal deficits depending on the location of the bleed. The patients’ eyes are sore and photophobia is present. Seizures occur in 20% of patients. A sentinel bleed prior to the rupture of an aneurysm occurs in a significant proportion of patients. There is controversy whether enlargement of the aneurysm with stretch of the dura can cause a sentinel headache. Clearly at surgery there are often signs of hemosiderin and a prior bleed.**

【203】**Familial aneurysm， polycystic kidney disease， Turner’s syndrome and associated AVM are clear clinical settings for aneurysm. Acquired aneurysms have been noted both with trauma， atrial myxoma and SBE (mycotic) on peripheral ar-teries. Cigarette smoking and vasculitis may predispose at the circle of Willis. The role of hypertension in causation is controversial， but not in regard to rupture. Some autopsy series have demonstrated 0.9% of patients with a congenital aneurysm. An aneurysm of 7-10 mm is the most likely to bleed. Those less than 3 mm in general do not. An infundibu-lum at the take off of cerebral arteries is usually less than2 mm and do not bleed.**

【204】**The use of coiling and interventional neuro-radioquaphic techniques has made aneurysm care much safer and success-ful for many patients. Unfortunately， vasospasm is still a ma-jor problem. The differential diagnosis for subarachnoid hem-orrhage is wide and includes vascular malformations as well as trauma， congophilic angiopathy， hemostasis dysfunction and diseases of the blood vessel wall.**

【16】The causes of lower quadrant pain or dysfunction vary widely； presentation of symptoms is equally wide ranging. Vascular conditions (e.g.， arterial insufficiency， abdominal aneurysm)， infectious or inflammatory conditions， gastro-intestinal (GI) disease， and gynecologic and male reproduc-tive systems may cause symptoms in the lower quadrant and lower extremity， including the pelvis， buttock， hip， groin， thigh， and knee. Some overlap may occur， but unique dif-ferences exist.

【17】Cancer may present as primary hip， groin， or leg pain or symptoms. Primary cancer can metastasize to the low back， pelvis， and sacrum， thus referring pain to the hip and groin. Primary cancer may also metastasize to the hip， causing hip or groin pain and related symptoms.

【18】Pain may be referred from other locations such as the scrotum， kidneys， abdominal wall， abdomen， peritoneum， or retroperitoneal region. Lower quadrant pain may be referred through conditions that affect nearby anatomic structures， such as the spine， spinal nerve roots， or peripheral nerves， and overlying soft tissue structures (e.g.， hernia， bursitis， fasciitis).2

【19】One of the keys to accurate and quick screening is knowl-edge of the types of conditions， illnesses， and systemic disor-ders that can refer pain to the lower quadrant， especially the hip and groin. Much of the information related to screening of the back ， sacrum， sacroiliac (SI)， and pel-vis  also applies to the hip and groin.

【20】**USING THE SCREENING MODEL TO EVALUATE THE LOWER QUADRANT**

【21】When screening is called for， the therapist looks at the client’s personal and family history， clinical presentation， and associated signs and symptoms. Knowledge of problems that can affect the lower quadrant， along with the likely history， pain patterns， and associated signs and symptoms， should guide the therapist with regard to the steps they should follow during screening.

Most often， the screening process takes place through a series of special questions. A few special tests may be used as well. Recognition of red-flag signs and symptoms of sys-temic or viscerogenic problems can direct the client toward|删除0换行|the necessary medical attention early in the disease process. In many cases， early detection and treatment may result in improved outcomes.

【23】**Past Medical History**

【24】Some of the more common histories associated with lower extremity， hip， or groin pain of a visceral nature are listed in Box 16.1. A previous history of cancer， such as prostate can-cer (men)， reproductive cancer (women)， or breast cancer， is a red flag as these cancers may be associated with metastases to the hip.

【25】Past history of joint replacement (especially hip arthro-plasty) combined with recent infection of any kind and new onset of hip， groin， or knee pain is suspicious. Postopera-tively， orthopedic pins may migrate， referring pain from the hip to the back， tibia， or ankle. Loose components，improper implant size， muscular imbalance， and infection that occur any time after joint arthroplasty may cause lower quadrant pain or symptoms (Case Example 16.1).

【26】There have been reports of hip， groin， and/or pelvic pain and/or mass associated with wear debris from hip arthro-plasty. Polyethylene wear debris can also cause deep vein thrombosis，lower extremity edema， ureteral or bladder com-pression， or sciatic neuropathy.

【15】**Screening the Lower Quadrant： Buttock， Hip， Groin，Thigh， and Leg**

【16】The causes of lower quadrant pain or dysfunction vary widely； presentation of symptoms is equally wide ranging. Vascular conditions (e.g.， arterial insufficiency， abdominal aneurysm)， infectious or inflammatory conditions， gastro-intestinal (GI) disease， and gynecologic and male reproduc-tive systems may cause symptoms in the lower quadrant and lower extremity， including the pelvis， buttock， hip， groin， thigh， and knee. Some overlap may occur， but unique dif-ferences exist.

【17】Cancer may present as primary hip， groin， or leg pain or symptoms. Primary cancer can metastasize to the low back， pelvis， and sacrum， thus referring pain to the hip and groin. Primary cancer may also metastasize to the hip， causing hip or groin pain and related symptoms.

【18】Pain may be referred from other locations such as the scrotum， kidneys， abdominal wall， abdomen， peritoneum， or retroperitoneal region. Lower quadrant pain may be referred through conditions that affect nearby anatomic structures， such as the spine， spinal nerve roots， or peripheral nerves， and overlying soft tissue structures (e.g.， hernia， bursitis， fasciitis).2

【19】One of the keys to accurate and quick screening is knowl-edge of the types of conditions， illnesses， and systemic disor-ders that can refer pain to the lower quadrant， especially the hip and groin. Much of the information related to screening of the back ， sacrum， sacroiliac (SI)， and pel-vis  also applies to the hip and groin.

【20】**USING THE SCREENING MODEL TO EVALUATE THE LOWER QUADRANT**

【21】When screening is called for， the therapist looks at the client’s personal and family history， clinical presentation， and associated signs and symptoms. Knowledge of problems that can affect the lower quadrant， along with the likely history， pain patterns， and associated signs and symptoms， should guide the therapist with regard to the steps they should follow during screening.

Most often， the screening process takes place through a series of special questions. A few special tests may be used as well. Recognition of red-flag signs and symptoms of sys-temic or viscerogenic problems can direct the client toward|删除0换行|the necessary medical attention early in the disease process. In many cases， early detection and treatment may result in improved outcomes.

【23】**Past Medical History**

【24】Some of the more common histories associated with lower extremity， hip， or groin pain of a visceral nature are listed in Box 16.1. A previous history of cancer， such as prostate can-cer (men)， reproductive cancer (women)， or breast cancer， is a red flag as these cancers may be associated with metastases to the hip.

【25】Past history of joint replacement (especially hip arthro-plasty) combined with recent infection of any kind and new onset of hip， groin， or knee pain is suspicious. Postopera-tively， orthopedic pins may migrate， referring pain from the hip to the back， tibia， or ankle. Loose components，improper implant size， muscular imbalance， and infection that occur any time after joint arthroplasty may cause lower quadrant pain or symptoms (Case Example 16.1).

【26】There have been reports of hip， groin， and/or pelvic pain and/or mass associated with wear debris from hip arthro-plasty. Polyethylene wear debris can also cause deep vein thrombosis，lower extremity edema， ureteral or bladder com-pression， or sciatic neuropathy.

【27】**Risk Factors**

【28】Each condition， illness， or disease that can cause referred pain to the buttock， hip， thigh， groin， or lower extremity has its own unique risk factors. Many of the items listed as past medical history are risk factors. For example， femoral artery catheterization used to monitor ongoing hemodynamic sta-tus (arterial line； status post burn injuries， and/or individu-als in the intensive care unit \[ICU\]) or used for individuals with poor upper extremity intravenous access can cause retroperitoneal hematoma formation or septic arthritis and subsequent hip pain. Complications from femoral artery catheterization are rare (0.81%) and most likely to occur in older adults.删除14:<u>4</u>

【15】**Screening the Lower Quadrant： Buttock， Hip， Groin，Thigh， and Leg**

【16】The causes of lower quadrant pain or dysfunction vary widely； presentation of symptoms is equally wide ranging. Vascular conditions (e.g.， arterial insufficiency， abdominal aneurysm)， infectious or inflammatory conditions， gastro-intestinal (GI) disease， and gynecologic and male reproduc-tive systems may cause symptoms in the lower quadrant and lower extremity， including the pelvis， buttock， hip， groin， thigh， and knee. Some overlap may occur， but unique dif-ferences exist.

【17】Cancer may present as primary hip， groin， or leg pain or symptoms. Primary cancer can metastasize to the low back， pelvis， and sacrum， thus referring pain to the hip and groin. Primary cancer may also metastasize to the hip， causing hip or groin pain and related symptoms.

【18】Pain may be referred from other locations such as the scrotum， kidneys， abdominal wall， abdomen， peritoneum， or retroperitoneal region. Lower quadrant pain may be referred through conditions that affect nearby anatomic structures， such as the spine， spinal nerve roots， or peripheral nerves， and overlying soft tissue structures (e.g.， hernia， bursitis， fasciitis).2

【19】One of the keys to accurate and quick screening is knowl-edge of the types of conditions， illnesses， and systemic disor-ders that can refer pain to the lower quadrant， especially the hip and groin. Much of the information related to screening of the back ， sacrum， sacroiliac (SI)， and pel-vis  also applies to the hip and groin.

【20】**USING THE SCREENING MODEL TO EVALUATE THE LOWER QUADRANT**

【21】When screening is called for， the therapist looks at the client’s personal and family history， clinical presentation， and associated signs and symptoms. Knowledge of problems that can affect the lower quadrant， along with the likely history， pain patterns， and associated signs and symptoms， should guide the therapist with regard to the steps they should follow during screening.

Most often， the screening process takes place through a series of special questions. A few special tests may be used as well. Recognition of red-flag signs and symptoms of sys-temic or viscerogenic problems can direct the client toward|删除0换行|the necessary medical attention early in the disease process. In many cases， early detection and treatment may result in improved outcomes.

【23】**Past Medical History**

【24】Some of the more common histories associated with lower extremity， hip， or groin pain of a visceral nature are listed in Box 16.1. A previous history of cancer， such as prostate can-cer (men)， reproductive cancer (women)， or breast cancer， is a red flag as these cancers may be associated with metastases to the hip.

【25】Past history of joint replacement (especially hip arthro-plasty) combined with recent infection of any kind and new onset of hip， groin， or knee pain is suspicious. Postopera-tively， orthopedic pins may migrate， referring pain from the hip to the back， tibia， or ankle. Loose components，improper implant size， muscular imbalance， and infection that occur any time after joint arthroplasty may cause lower quadrant pain or symptoms (Case Example 16.1).

【26】There have been reports of hip， groin， and/or pelvic pain and/or mass associated with wear debris from hip arthro-plasty. Polyethylene wear debris can also cause deep vein thrombosis，lower extremity edema， ureteral or bladder com-pression， or sciatic neuropathy.

【27】**Risk Factors**

【28】Each condition， illness， or disease that can cause referred pain to the buttock， hip， thigh， groin， or lower extremity has its own unique risk factors. Many of the items listed as past medical history are risk factors. For example， femoral artery catheterization used to monitor ongoing hemodynamic sta-tus (arterial line； status post burn injuries， and/or individu-als in the intensive care unit \[ICU\]) or used for individuals with poor upper extremity intravenous access can cause retroperitoneal hematoma formation or septic arthritis and subsequent hip pain. Complications from femoral artery catheterization are rare (0.81%) and most likely to occur in older adults.删除14:<u>4</u>

【38】**Hip and Buttock**

【39】The physical therapist is well acquainted with hip or buttock pain  that occurs as a result of regional neuro-muscular or musculoskeletal disorders. The therapist must be aware that disorders affecting the organs within the pelvic and abdominal cavities can also refer pain to the hip region， mimicking a primary musculoskeletal lesion. A careful his-tory and physical examination usually differentiate these entities from true hip disease.删除14:<u>6</u>

【40】Pain Pattern. True hip pain， whether from a neuromusculo-skeletal or systemic cause ， is usualy felt posteriorly deep within the buttock or anteriorly in the groin， sometimes with radiating pain down the anterior thigh. Pain perceived on the outer (lateral) side or posterior aspect of the hip is usually not caused by an intraarticular problem but more likely results from a trigger point， bursitis， knee， SI， or back problem.

【41】With true hip joint disease， pain will occur with active or passive motion of the hip joint； this pain increases with weight-bearing.Often， an antalgic gait pattern is observed as the individual leans away from the affected hip and shortens the swing phase to avoid weight-bearing.

【42】When the underlying problem is related to soft tissue (e.g.， abductor weakness) rather than to the joint as the source of symptoms， the client may lean toward the affected side to com-pensate for the downward rotation of the pelvis. With soft tis-sue involvement of the bursa or tendons (e.g， gluteus medius， gluteus minimus) pain may radiate from the buttock， greater trochanter， and/or lateral thigh down the leg to the level of insertion of the iliotibial tract on the proximal tibia.<mark>-11</mark>

【50】Etiology and pathogenesis. The lips and the palate orig-inate from the first branchial arch between the 7th and the 12th week of gestation. 【65】**Molecular Pathology Methods Introduction**

【66】**Molecular-based methods are now standard aids in the diagnosis of a variety of pathologic conditions. Ongoing advances in molecular pathology， genomics， epigenomics， proteomics，and infectious diseases research， as well as tech-nologic developments， will serve to further the battery of molecular assays available for improved disease characteri-zation and patient care. This section reviews a wide range of molecular pathology techniques that can be adaptable for application in surgical pathology practice. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and in situ hybridization (ISH) have widespread clinical use.**

【67】**Nucleic Acid Extraction Methods**

【68】**The extraction of nucleic acids from pathology samples involves cell lysis followed by selective DNA or RNA isolation， and a quantity and quality assessment relative to the requirements of the end-diagnostic test**

【69】Pathology samples that can be used for molecular analysis include tissue samples (fresh or formalin-fixed， paraffin-embedded \[FFPE\])； bodily fluidsamniotic fluid， saliva， stools， urine， buccal and cervical scrapes； fine-needle aspirates； hair root； peripheral blood： and cell cultures

【70】**DNA extraction methods**

【71】\- Classic methods were time-consuming (about 3days) and required relatively large quantities of tissues (100 mg to>l g)

【72】—Numerous extraction kits are now available that use glass-fiber filters that selectively bind DNA after tissue treatments with a protease and chaotropic buffers (which disrupt protein and DNA secondary structures). The glass fibers， typically loaded in mini-columns， are washed to rinse away cellular debris， extraction solution reagents，and pathology tissue processing chemicals. The DNA is then recovered from the resin or glass-fiber by low- _1.T_ salt buffer rinses. Pure DNA recovery from diverse pathology samples is possible within several hours by these procedures

【73】**_—_ Automated DNA extraction platforms are available for the processing of multiple patient samples**

【74】**RNA extraction methods**

【75】**\- Classic methods required the rapid homogenization of large quantities of fresh tissues in protease and guanidinium thiocyanate solution to denature ubiquitous endogenous RNases that otherwise degrade cellular RNA**

【76】Current methods allow the relatively rapid(1-day) recovery of RNA， again after tissue homogenization in a chaotropic guanidinium salt solution that leaves RNA contained in an aqueous phase and protein and DNA in an organic phase. Admixture of the aqueous phase with nucleic acid-binding glass filters allows recovery of pure total RNA by elution from the glass filters with a low-salt buffer. Messenger RNA(mRNA) can be purified from total RNA by passage through oligo(dT) cellulose spin columns.Mini-columns have been developed for the extraction of RNA from all types of pathology samples

【77】**DNA and RNA quantification， purity， and integrity assay**

【78】\- High-integrity nucleic acids are best extracted from fresh tissue specimens. Extraction from tissues preserved in liquid nitrogen is the next best option. Commercially available storage reagents (e.g.， RNAlater， Ambion， Inc.， Foster City， CA) preserve tissue morphology and nucleic acid integrity

【79】**DNA and RNA extracts from FFPE tissues tend to be degraded. In general， the quality of nucleic acids extractable from FFPE blocks decreases with block age**

【80】The concentration of extracted nucleic acids is assessed spectrophotometrically. Both DNA and RNA absorb UV light， with peak absorbance at a wavelength of 260 nm； an absorbance (A260) reading of 1.0 demonstrates a DNA concentration of 50 ug/mL or an RNA concentration of 40 ug/mL

【81】__ The purity of extracted DNA or RNA is also determined spectrophotometrically. Readings taken at A230 and at A270 are indicators of contamination with organics (such as guanidinium salts) and phenol， respectively.

【82】Contamination with proteins can be inferred from an A280 reading， at which peak protein absorbance occurs. Particulate matter contamination can ULLIS. be gauged from an A320 reading. Typically， an A(260-320)：A(280-320) ratio is calculated； a value of 1.7to 2.0 indicates pure DNA or RNA

【84】Nucleic acid integrity can be estimated by comparing nucleic acid fragment size against a molecular weight ladder after agarose gel electrophoresis. The presence of a smear extending to smaller fragments indicates degraded DNA. Total RNA integrity is gauged in terms of the presence of 28S (about 5 kb) and 18S (about2 kb) ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Discrete 28S and18S bands， with minimal smearing，indicate intact RNA species， whereas partial or absent bands and smeared rRNA indicate a degraded sample

【85】**Instruments such as the NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific， Wilmington，DE) and the Agilent 2100Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies Inc.， Santa Clara，CA) have facilitated rapid DNA and RNA quantitation and purity analyses，and RNA integrity assay， respectively**

【86】Nucleic acids storage

【87】**\- DNA is generally stored at 4℃ for assays performed within 1 week to l month of extraction. and in aliquots at-20°Cor-80°Cfor longer-term storage； repeated freeze-thawing may lead to DNA degradation**

【88】RNA is more labile than DNA and is susceptible to degradation by RNases that are a pervasive laboratory hazard. For short-term use， RNA is stored at-20°℃，and at-80℃ or under liquid nitrogen for longer-term use

【89】**Tissue Microdissection Methods**

【90】Background

【91】\- Microdissection enables the targeted collection of cells or tissues from slide-mounted cytologic specimens or frozen or FFPE tissues sections

【92】—Sample tissues may be treated for nucleic acids or protein extraction

【93】**Methods**

【94】\- In the simplest approach， lightly stained tissues sections are viewed by dissecting microscope， and after dampening the tissues with 70% ethanol， the tissues are selectively scraped off the slides using a syringe needle. DNA is extracted from the collected tissues after digestion with proteinase K. A glass-fiber mini-column method allows further purification

【65】**Molecular Pathology Methods Introduction**

【66】**Molecular-based methods are now standard aids in the diagnosis of a variety of pathologic conditions. Ongoing advances in molecular pathology， genomics， epigenomics， proteomics，and infectious diseases research， as well as tech-nologic developments， will serve to further the battery of molecular assays available for improved disease characteri-zation and patient care. This section reviews a wide range of molecular pathology techniques that can be adaptable for application in surgical pathology practice. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and in situ hybridization (ISH) have widespread clinical use.**

【67】**Nucleic Acid Extraction Methods**

【68】**The extraction of nucleic acids from pathology samples involves cell lysis followed by selective DNA or RNA isolation， and a quantity and quality assessment relative to the requirements of the end-diagnostic test**

【69】Pathology samples that can be used for molecular analysis include tissue samples (fresh or formalin-fixed， paraffin-embedded \[FFPE\])； bodily fluidsamniotic fluid， saliva， stools， urine， buccal and cervical scrapes； fine-needle aspirates； hair root； peripheral blood： and cell cultures

【70】**DNA extraction methods**

【71】\- Classic methods were time-consuming (about 3days) and required relatively large quantities of tissues (100 mg to>l g)

【72】—Numerous extraction kits are now available that use glass-fiber filters that selectively bind DNA after tissue treatments with a protease and chaotropic buffers (which disrupt protein and DNA secondary structures). The glass fibers， typically loaded in mini-columns， are washed to rinse away cellular debris， extraction solution reagents，and pathology tissue processing chemicals. The DNA is then recovered from the resin or glass-fiber by low- _1.T_ salt buffer rinses. Pure DNA recovery from diverse pathology samples is possible within several hours by these procedures

【73】**_—_ Automated DNA extraction platforms are available for the processing of multiple patient samples**

【74】**RNA extraction methods**

【75】**\- Classic methods required the rapid homogenization of large quantities of fresh tissues in protease and guanidinium thiocyanate solution to denature ubiquitous endogenous RNases that otherwise degrade cellular RNA**

【76】Current methods allow the relatively rapid(1-day) recovery of RNA， again after tissue homogenization in a chaotropic guanidinium salt solution that leaves RNA contained in an aqueous phase and protein and DNA in an organic phase. Admixture of the aqueous phase with nucleic acid-binding glass filters allows recovery of pure total RNA by elution from the glass filters with a low-salt buffer. Messenger RNA(mRNA) can be purified from total RNA by passage through oligo(dT) cellulose spin columns.Mini-columns have been developed for the extraction of RNA from all types of pathology samples

【77】**DNA and RNA quantification， purity， and integrity assay**

【78】\- High-integrity nucleic acids are best extracted from fresh tissue specimens. Extraction from tissues preserved in liquid nitrogen is the next best option. Commercially available storage reagents (e.g.， RNAlater， Ambion， Inc.， Foster City， CA) preserve tissue morphology and nucleic acid integrity

【79】**DNA and RNA extracts from FFPE tissues tend to be degraded. In general， the quality of nucleic acids extractable from FFPE blocks decreases with block age**

【80】The concentration of extracted nucleic acids is assessed spectrophotometrically. Both DNA and RNA absorb UV light， with peak absorbance at a wavelength of 260 nm； an absorbance (A260) reading of 1.0 demonstrates a DNA concentration of 50 ug/mL or an RNA concentration of 40 ug/mL

【81】__ The purity of extracted DNA or RNA is also determined spectrophotometrically. Readings taken at A230 and at A270 are indicators of contamination with organics (such as guanidinium salts) and phenol， respectively.

【82】Contamination with proteins can be inferred from an A280 reading， at which peak protein absorbance occurs. Particulate matter contamination can ULLIS. be gauged from an A320 reading. Typically， an A(260-320)：A(280-320) ratio is calculated； a value of 1.7to 2.0 indicates pure DNA or RNA

【83】零碎段删除-1:<u>**_—_**</u>

【84】Nucleic acid integrity can be estimated by comparing nucleic acid fragment size against a molecular weight ladder after agarose gel electrophoresis. The presence of a smear extending to smaller fragments indicates degraded DNA. Total RNA integrity is gauged in terms of the presence of 28S (about 5 kb) and 18S (about2 kb) ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Discrete 28S and18S bands， with minimal smearing，indicate intact RNA species， whereas partial or absent bands and smeared rRNA indicate a degraded sample

【85】**Instruments such as the NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific， Wilmington，DE) and the Agilent 2100Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies Inc.， Santa Clara，CA) have facilitated rapid DNA and RNA quantitation and purity analyses，and RNA integrity assay， respectively**

【86】Nucleic acids storage

【87】**\- DNA is generally stored at 4℃ for assays performed within 1 week to l month of extraction. and in aliquots at-20°Cor-80°Cfor longer-term storage； repeated freeze-thawing may lead to DNA degradation**

【88】RNA is more labile than DNA and is susceptible to degradation by RNases that are a pervasive laboratory hazard. For short-term use， RNA is stored at-20°℃，and at-80℃ or under liquid nitrogen for longer-term use

【91】\- Microdissection enables the targeted collection of cells or tissues from slide-mounted cytologic specimens or frozen or FFPE tissues sections

【93】**Methods**

【94】\- In the simplest approach， lightly stained tissues sections are viewed by dissecting microscope， and after dampening the tissues with 70% ethanol， the tissues are selectively scraped off the slides using a syringe needle. DNA is extracted from the collected tissues after digestion with proteinase K. A glass-fiber mini-column method allows further purification

【5】**DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【6】**Metastasis： This diagnosis is unlikely because the mass has a high lipid content， as evidenced by the loss of signal intensity on the opposed phase image. The T2valuc would likely be >60 ms in metastases.**

【7】**Pheochromocytoma： A much higher signal intensity on the T2-weighted image and， therefore， a longer calculat-ed T2 value would be expected in this diagnosis.**

【8】**Nonhyperfunctioning adenoma： This is the most likely diagnosis given the sizc and loss of signal intensi-ty on the opposed-phase images， even though the patient has a known malignancy.**

【9】** DIAGNOSIS： Nonhyperfunctioning adenoma.**

【10】**e KEY FACTS _CLINICAL_**

【11】**Adrenocortical adenomas may be nonhyperfunctioning or hyperfunctioning. The incidence of nonhyperfunc-tioning adcnomas in the general population is 1% to3%.**

【12】**Hyperfunctioning adenomas may secrete：**

【13】**Cortisol： Cushing’s syndrome (adenoma are usually>4 cm in diameter)**

【14】**Aldosterone： Conn’s syndrome (adenomas are usually<2 cm in diameter)**

【15】**Androgens： virilization**

【16】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【17】**On CT， a precontrast attenuation value <0 Hounsficld units (HU) significs a benign condition； a precontrast attenuation value +1-10 HU signifies that the adeno-ma is likely benign and may warrant follow-up based on the clinical setting.**

【18】**COpposed-phase MRI results in lower signal of the lesion compared with conventional in-phase MRI due to intracytoplasmic lipid. Calculated T2 values are gen-erally <60 ms.**

【19】**Malignant imaging features include large size (>5 cm)， heterogeneity， intense contrast enhancement， and an increase in size on follow-up imaging.**

【20】**Imaging studies cannot differentiate hyperfunctioning from nonhyperfunctioning adenomas.**

【28】**\*DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【29】**\]Endometrial carcinoma with extension to the uter-ine cervix： This should be the primary consideration in this postmenopausal patient.**

【30】**】Endometrial polyp： This is a possibility； however， polyps typically appear more focal and round. Only when it is surrounded by endometrial fluid can one make the definitive diagnosis of a polyp.**

【31】**Endometrial hyperplasia： This entity can be impossi-ble to differentiatc from cndometrial carcinoma when the disease proccss is confined to the uterus. However， the disease proccss in this case clearly extends into the cervix， making endometrial hyperplasia very unlikely.**

【32】** Retained placenta with hemorrhage or pus： These processes tend to be more heterogeneous and， of course， would not be supported by the history.**

【33】**IInvasive molar pregnancy： This would also be a con-sidcration in a patient with the appropriate history and elevated human chorionic gonadotropin values.**

【34】**DIAGNOSIS： Endometrial carcinoma with inva-sion of the myometrium and cervix， FIGO stage II.**

【35】**KEY FACTS _CLINICAL_**

【36】**_AAlthough 80% of cases of endometrial carcinoma occur_ in postmenopausal women， 90% of postmenopausal bleeding is caused by benign disease.**

【37】**FEndometrial carcinoma is staged as follows according to the FIGO system：**

【38】人名段删除-1:<u>**_Stage_ _Description_**</u>

【39】**IConfined to the uterine corpus **

【40】**Confined to the endometrium**

【41】**Invasion confined to the inner 50% of the myomctrium**

【42】**IC Invasion extends into the outer 50% of the mvometrium**

【43】**ⅡExtension to the uterine ccrvix Extrauterine spread limited to the true pclvis**

【44】**_IVA_ Extension to the bladder or rectum**

【45】**_IVB_ Distant metastases**

【46】**The incidence of pclvic lymph node involvement increases dramatically with stage IC and II lesions.**

【47】**Endometrial carcinoma can be cither focal or diffuse. The current case is a good example of diffuse diseasc.**

【48】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【49】**Ultrasound is somewhat limited in its ability to distin-guish between endometrial carcinoma and other causes of endometrial thickening.**

**The accepted rangc of normal for endometrial thick-ness， as determined by adding the measurements of thc|删除0换行|anterior and posterior components of the endometri-um， depends on the hormonal status of the patient，as follows：**

【51】**_Hormonal status_ _Normal range_ Premenopausal Proliferative phasc 4 to 8 mm Secretory phase 7 to 14 mm Postmcnopausal Without estrogen replacement 4 to 8 mm With estrogen rcplacement <10mm**

【52】** In two studies of patients with postmenopausal bleed ing， no patient with an endometrial thickness of <5mm had malignant pathology.**

【53】**On sagittal T2-weighted MR images， the junctional zone will clearly separate the endometrium from the myometrium in most patients. Disruption of the junc-tional zone is evidence for invasion into the myometri-um. However， approximately 50% of postmenopausal womcn will not have a visible junctional zone on T2-weighted images. The use of gadolinium-cnhanced dynamic imaging produces improved contrast between the enhancing endometrial carcinoma and the even more strongly enhancing myometrium. Because endometrial carcinoma enhances more than normal endometrium， superficial lesions are more easily rccog-nized after enhancement. The junctional zone can also be delineated better using this technique.**

【54】**The accuracy of endovaginal ultrasound and MRI， using T2-weighted imaging， in the determination of the depth of myometrial invasion is approximatcly76%. The recent use of contrast-enhanced dynamic MRI of the uterus has increased the accuracy to approximately 90% in the best hands.**

【75】**\*DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【76】**Iliopsoas bursitis (IPB)： The location of the mass anterior to the hip joint， lateral to the femoral vessels， and deep to the psoas tendon， the teardrop or round configuration， and its fluid signal intensity characteris-tics are in favor of this diagnosis. The associated effu-sion indicates communication of the bursa with the hip joint. The cystic nature can be depicted further with Tl-weighted gadolinium-enhanced MRI. The wall of the inflamed bursa would be expected to enhance uni-formly without nodularity， while the fluid will not enhance. Other studies documented a seronegative arthropathy.**

【77】**Neoplasm： Most tumors have a heterogeneous signal intensity pattern. Tl-weighted gadolinium-enhanced MRI helps differentiate tumors like intramuscular myx-oma， synovial sarcoma， and hemangioma， which can imitate bursitis.**

【78】**Femoral hernia： Lack of gas and the signal characteris-tics indicating fluid in this mass exclude this condition.**

【79】**Abscess： Intramuscular abscess can be excluded because the collection of fluid is not intramuscular. However， in general， septic bursitis cannot be excluded unless nonin-fected fluid is obtained by percutaneous aspiration.**

【80】**Femoral artery aneurysm： Normal femoral vessels are seen in this patient. Furthermore， the location， fluid nature， age of the patient， and the communication with joint space are not consistent with this diagnosis.**

【81】**DIAGNOSIS： Iliopsoas bursitis associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathy.**

【82】** KEY FACTS**

【83】**_CLINICAL_**

【84】**The iliopsoas bursa is the largest bursa in the body and is present in 98% of adults， interposed between the illa-cus muscle/psoas tendon and the anterior capsule of the hip， lateral to the femoral artery， vein， and nerve. Communication exists between the iliopsoas bursa and the hip joint in 14% of adults.**

【85】**_I_ Inflammation and enlargement of the iliopsoas bursa may occur secondary to hip joint disease or， occasion-ally， as a primary bursal process.**

【86】**Diseases associated with IPB include seropositive and seronegative arthropathies， osteoarthritis， pigmented vil-lonodular synovitis， synovial chondromatosis， infection， hip prosthesis， occupational trauma， and sports injuries.**

【87】**Clinical presentation in IPB includes pain， mass lesion， and compression syndromes of the inguinal compart-ment (pseudothrombophlebitis， femoral nervc neu-ropathy that may simulate L4 radiculopathy). Retroperitoncal extension of the iliopsoas bursa may present as a palpable abdominal or pelvic mass.**

【88】**IPB is frequently confused with a femoral hernia， lymphadenopathy， neoplasms， or a femoral artery aneurysm.**

【89】** Therapy for IPB is variable. Rest and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are indicated for mild cases. Aspiration and corticosteroid injection may be required in more severe cases. Occasionally， surgical resection of the bursa is necessary.**

【90】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【91】**Early， accurate diagnosis of IPB is facilitated by appro-priate radiologic studies.**

【92】**Conventional radiographs can help assess underlying hip joint disorders such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.**

【93】**Ultrasound may demonstrate the fluid-filled nature of palpable lesions and can guide needle aspiration1.**

【94】**Contrast bursography outlines the extent of bursal enlargement.**

【95】**Hip arthrography is definitive in establishing the diag-nosis when a communication exists.**

【96】**On CT， a water attenuation mass is typically scen in close apposition to the tendon muscle at the level of the hip joint and lateral to the femoral vessels. When a com-munication exists， an associated hip effusion may be seen. If the bursitis is secondary to a hip arthropathy， evidence of osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis may be seen. Intravenous contrast matcrial enhances the wall of the bursa but not the contents， as expected for a fluid collection in an inflamed bursa. In primary IPB， the hip joint may be normal. If there is no communication with the joint， there will be no evidence of a hip effusion.**

【97】**__ The soft-tissue contrast， noninvasiveness， and multiplanar capability of MRI make it superior for assessing IPB. Underlying arthropathic changes can be characterized in a case of secondary IPB. The signal intensity of uncom-plicated bursitis is that of fluid. Debris， loose bodies， or blood yield different signal intensities. Contrast enhance ment of the inflamed wall due to hypervascularity is typi-cally seen. Signal intensity in synovial chondromatosis of the iliopsoas bursa varies depending on the degrec of cal-cification of the cartilaginous nodules. However， in pig-mented villonodular IPB， the hemosiderin will typically be of low signal intensity on all sequences.**

【98】**MRI wil! make the positive diagnosis of IPB in most clinical situations and exclude othcr conditions such as a hernia， tumor， lymph node， hematoma， aneurysm， and abscess. Ultrasound or CT-guided bursal aspira-tion can exclude septic bursitis， detect the presence of crystals， and provide a means of drainage of the bursa and injection of corticosteroids.**

【103】**DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS**

【104】** Pronation-abduction injury： This is an uncommon fracture pattern characterized by a low， oblique fibular fracture at the level of the ankle joint.**

【105】**Supination-external rotation (SER) injury： These injuries are characterized by a long oblique fracturc of the distal fibula usually measuring 2 to 4 cm in length. Not uncommonly， the fracture is most apparent on the lateral view of the ankle.**

【106】**Supination-adduction injury： This injury causes a horizontally oriented fracture in the distal fibula， usu-ally below the joint line.**

【107】** Pronation-external rotation injury： This injury pro-duces a relatively horizontal fracture of the fibular dia-physis approximately 5 to 8 cm above the ankle joint.**

【108】**DIAGNOSIS： Supination-external rotation injury.**

【109】**KEY FACTS**

【110】**_CLINICAL_**

【111】**SER is the most commonly observed ankle fracture pattern.**

【112】**The fracturc is preceded by ankle inversion and rup ture of the anterior tibiofibular ligament.**

【113】**Asymmetric widening of the ankle mortise denotes instability， an indication for open reduction with inter-nal fixation.**

【114】**_RADIOLOGIC_**

【115】**There is typically a long (2 to 4 cm)， oblique-spiral fracture of the distal fibula.**

【116】**The fracture is often seen best on the lateral view.**

【117】**SER injury may be associated with cither or both pos-terior and medial malleolus fractures or a tear of the deltoid ligament.**

【118】**The patterns of ankle fractures described in the differ-ential diagnosis arc derived from the Lauge-Hansen classification system. Although other classification schemes exist， it is the most widely uscd for communi cating radiographic findings， determining appropriate orthopedic therapy， and predicting the prognosis.**

【119】**__ The importance of the classification system is the recognition that ankle fractures are not randomly ori-entcd fractures through the medial， lateral， and poste-rior malleoli， but rather occur in a stereotypical and prcdictable manner based on the mechanism of injury， the position of the foot and ankle at the time of injury， and the relative strength and weakness of the bony and ligamentous structures about the ankle.**

【120】**The four types of fractures cause a relatively unique pat-tern of injury to the fibula， which is so characteristic it allows one to easily classify the four fracture types.**

【21】开头批量删除-1:<u>**It is remarkable that until recently sonographic studies of the bowel have not reached the diagnostic level that sonography has attained for other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Gas posed the major ob-stacle to obtaining consistent quality results. Julien Puylaert has de-veloped a graded-compression technique which is not only able to eliminate gas artifacts， but also - by reducing the distance between the transducer and the bowel- allows the use of high-frequency transducers. 【88】页码间删除-1:<u>**1 Introduction**</u>

【89】**On the 18th of June， 1886， at the inaugural meeting of the Association of American Physicians， Dr. Reginald Fitz presented a study titled“Perforating inflammation of the vermiform appendix， with special reference to its early diagnosis and treatment." This study was to be-come a classic in the history of medicine. Fitz was the first to recog-nize that the feared condition previously known as perityphlitis， as well as all its variants， in fact originated from one entity： inflamma-tion of the vermiform appendix. He coined the term “appendicitis”and was the first to advocate early appendectomy as the treatment of choice.**

【90】**In the ensuing years appendectomy became a routine procedure all over the world and the mortality from appendicitis rapidly de-creased. A further decrease in mortality followed the introduction of antibiotics and better anesthetic procedures after World War II.**

【91】**Although appendectomy has been universally accepted as the treatment of choice for appendicitis， the correct diagnosis of this common disease has remained elusive. The diagnosis is as often wrongly made as it is overlooked， the first leading to an unnecessary operation， the second to ill-advised delay. False-positive and false-negative diagnoses both arise at a frequency of approximately 25%and the efforts to improve diagnostic accuracy have been as fruitless as they are countless. Especially in the field of radiology no single di-agnostic method has gained universal acceptance. Diagnosis and therapy still depend largely on history， physical examination， and a few simple laboratory tests.**

【92】**An incidental sonographic finding in a patient in our hospital prompted a study on the value of ultrasound in the diagnosis of ap-pendicitis， the first results of which were published in Radiology in1986. This book reflects a 4-year experience with ultrasound exami-nation in patients with clinical signs of appendicitis.**

【93】**The appendix is the vermiform continuation of the caecum and arises from its posteromedial aspect. It may occupy any position： directed medially (35%)， caudally (30%)， laterally (10%)， or retrocaecally(25%). In the retrocaecal position the appendix may occasionally be situated retroperitoneally. The average length of the appendix is9 cm， and if the lumen is collapsed the average diameter is 4.5 mm. Starting from the lumen， the wall of the appendix  consists of mucosa， submucosa， muscularis， and serosa. The mucosa comprises an epithelial surface and the lamina propria which contains lym-phoid follicles. The muscularis mucosae is often deficient， which ren-ders the transition to the submucosa indistinct. The submucosa is made up of loose connective tissue containing multiple small vessels. Although an immunological role has been suggested， the function of the appendix is still unknown.**

【94】页码间删除-1:<u>**2.2 Pathophysiology**</u>

【95】**The etiology of acute appendicitis is obstruction， followed by infection. Wangensteen and Dennis (1940) performed experiments with animal appendices， which they ligated at the base after milking some feces from the caecum into the lumen of the appendix. Invariably this procedure resulted in a pathological condition indistinguishable from human appendicitis. He was also able to measure an increase of in-traluminal pressure of an experimentally obstructed human appen-dix. It has been accepted ever since that obstruction is the most im-**

通用删除16(英):<u>**Fig. 2.1. Layers of the appendix wall**</u>|删除换行|portant， probably the only etiological factor precipitating appendici-tis.**

【97】**Whereas the role of obstruction as the main cause of appendicitis is not challenged， the reasons for the obstruction are controversial. It seems hard to clarify this matter since the base of the appendix， which is often the level of obstruction， is inverted into the caecum during the operation and thus not accessible to pathological verifica-tion.**

【98】**It is accepted that in 35% of all patients the presence of a fecolith plays an important role in the pathological process 删除1:<u>(Shaw 1965)</u>. However， whether the fecolith is the prime originator of the obstruc-tive process or whether it modifies progression after the disease has started is still a matter of speculation. The lamination of most feco-liths clearly indicates that they can be present for a long time without causing any problems. Lymphoid hyperplasia has been implicated as the principal reason for obstruction 删除1:<u>(Bohrod 1946)</u>. This view is sup-ported by the increased incidence of appendicitis observed during outbreaks of measles and mononucleosis 删除1:<u>(Schrock 1983)</u>. Scar tissue due to previous inflammation may be the precipitating factor in at-tacks of recurrent appendicitis 删除1:<u>(Condon 1977)</u>. A functional obstruc-tion， caused by high intraluminal pressure in the caecum - analogous to the pathophysiological mechanism of diverticulitis - has been pro-posed as the main cause of appendicitis. This view is supported by the observation that appendicitis is rare in populations on a high re-sidual diet 删除1:<u>(Burkitt 1971)</u>.**

【99】**Foreign bodies， tumors， parasites， and gall stones are reported as rare causes of obstruction in appendicitis.**

【100】**Bacterial invasion in the absence of obstruction seems unlikely to be the primary etiological agent， since the bacteria found in appendi-citis do not cause small - or large - bowel perforation either unless there is obstruction. There are a few reports on true appendicitis asso-ciated with bacterial enteritis by enteropathogenic microorganisms. However， this is more likely the result of mechanical obstruction of the appendiceal lumen due to the associated hyperplasia of the lym-phoid tissue 删除1:<u>(Rubenstein and Johnson 1945； Sjostrom 1971)</u>.**

【101】**A vascular type of appendiceal perforation may exist theoreti-cally， in which the primary lesion is ischemia and not obstruction删除1:<u>(Robbins 1974)</u>.**

【102】**Once the appendiceal lumen is obstructed and if the patient is not operated upon soon， there are various pathophysiological path-ways open . In the presence of obstruction continuous mu-cus secretion will cause an increase of the intraluminal pressure and a subsequent stretching of the visceral peritoneum. This is perceived by the patient as visceral pain， localized in the periumbilical or epigastric area. After a while the inflamed serosa touches the parietal perito-neum causing localized pain， responsible for the well-known shift of pain to the right lower abdomen.**

【103】**If at this point the obstruction is relieved spontaneously， appen-dicitis runs an abortive course， and clinical symptoms will rather sud-denly subside.**
