【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【6】**·These features are mainly focused on longer periods of recommended observation relative to the patient’s age as outlined below.**

【7】**1 Coma and apnea must co-exist.**

【8】**2 Absence of brainstem function**

【9】2.1 Pupils unreactive to light (midposition or dilated).

【10】2.2 Absence of spontaneous eye movement， or in response to oculocephalic and oculovestibular testing.

【11】2.3 Absence of movement of bulbar musculature， including facial and oro-pharyngeal muscles (corneal，gag， cough，sucking， and rooting reflexes).

【12】2.4 Respiratory movements are absent with patient off the respirator.

【13】2.5 Apnea testing using standardized methods'can be performed.

【14】3 Absence of hypotension for age or hypothermia.

【15】4 Flaccid muscle tone， absence of spontaneous movements (excluding spinal re-flexes).

【175】**Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies**

【176】**·Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is nearly exclusively maternally inherited.**

【177】**· mtDNA is a closed， circular DNA molecule consisting of ~16，000nucleotides coding for 37 genes.**

【178】**· Every cell contains multiple mitochondria with multiple copies of DNA， a condition known as polyplasmy.**

【179】**·Mitochondrial diseases demonstrate a threshold effect， whereby disease onset and severity are a function of the balance between the proportion of mutant and wild-type mtDNAs.**

【180】**·May involve multiple tissues with high energy requirements-such as brain， retina， muscle， cochlea，etc.**

【182】**Diseases due to trinucleotide repeat expansions**

【183】**·Unstable expansion of trinucleotide repeats is the mechanism underlying disorders featuring anticipation， the tendency for subsequent generations to be affected at an earlier age and with increased severity.**

【184】**· The molecular mechanisms of disease are poorly understood as the triplet expansions are known to be located in coding sequences (Huntington disease)， non-coding sequences (Friedreich ataxia)， 5'-untranslated regions(fragile X syndrome)，and 3'-untranslated regions (myotonic dystrophy).**

【185】**·CAG repeat expansions that encode polyglutamines appear to result in protein misfolding， a recuring theme in many of these disorders.**

【186】**·DNA molecular diagnostic tests are available. However， estimating disease onset and severity within an individual is not accurately predicted by absolute repeat number. Therefore， great care must be taken to ensure accurate information is provided when using molecular data in genetic counseling， particularly in asymptomatic individuals.**

【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【6】**·These features are mainly focused on longer periods of recommended observation relative to the patient’s age as outlined below.**

【7】**1 Coma and apnea must co-exist.**

【8】**2 Absence of brainstem function**

【9】2.1 Pupils unreactive to light (midposition or dilated).

【10】2.2 Absence of spontaneous eye movement， or in response to oculocephalic and oculovestibular testing.

【11】2.3 Absence of movement of bulbar musculature， including facial and oro-pharyngeal muscles (corneal，gag， cough，sucking， and rooting reflexes).

【12】2.4 Respiratory movements are absent with patient off the respirator.

【13】2.5 Apnea testing using standardized methods'can be performed.

【14】3 Absence of hypotension for age or hypothermia.

【15】4 Flaccid muscle tone， absence of spontaneous movements (excluding spinal re-flexes).

【16】5 Examination consistent with brain death throughout the period of testing and observation.

【175】**Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies**

【176】**·Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is nearly exclusively maternally inherited.**

【177】**· mtDNA is a closed， circular DNA molecule consisting of ~16，000nucleotides coding for 37 genes.**

【178】**· Every cell contains multiple mitochondria with multiple copies of DNA， a condition known as polyplasmy.**

【179】**·Mitochondrial diseases demonstrate a threshold effect， whereby disease onset and severity are a function of the balance between the proportion of mutant and wild-type mtDNAs.**

【180】**·May involve multiple tissues with high energy requirements-such as brain， retina， muscle， cochlea，etc.**

【182】**Diseases due to trinucleotide repeat expansions**

【183】**·Unstable expansion of trinucleotide repeats is the mechanism underlying disorders featuring anticipation， the tendency for subsequent generations to be affected at an earlier age and with increased severity.**

【184】**· The molecular mechanisms of disease are poorly understood as the triplet expansions are known to be located in coding sequences (Huntington disease)， non-coding sequences (Friedreich ataxia)， 5'-untranslated regions(fragile X syndrome)，and 3'-untranslated regions (myotonic dystrophy).**

【185】**·CAG repeat expansions that encode polyglutamines appear to result in protein misfolding， a recuring theme in many of these disorders.**

【186】**·DNA molecular diagnostic tests are available. However， estimating disease onset and severity within an individual is not accurately predicted by absolute repeat number. 【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【6】**·These features are mainly focused on longer periods of recommended observation relative to the patient’s age as outlined below.**

【7】**1 Coma and apnea must co-exist.**

【8】**2 Absence of brainstem function**

【9】2.1 Pupils unreactive to light (midposition or dilated).

【10】2.2 Absence of spontaneous eye movement， or in response to oculocephalic and oculovestibular testing.

【11】2.3 Absence of movement of bulbar musculature， including facial and oro-pharyngeal muscles (corneal，gag， cough，sucking， and rooting reflexes).

【12】2.4 Respiratory movements are absent with patient off the respirator.

【13】2.5 Apnea testing using standardized methods'can be performed.

【14】3 Absence of hypotension for age or hypothermia.

【175】**Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies**

【176】**·Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is nearly exclusively maternally inherited.**

【177】**· mtDNA is a closed， circular DNA molecule consisting of ~16，000nucleotides coding for 37 genes.**

【178】**· Every cell contains multiple mitochondria with multiple copies of DNA， a condition known as polyplasmy.**

【179】**·Mitochondrial diseases demonstrate a threshold effect， whereby disease onset and severity are a function of the balance between the proportion of mutant and wild-type mtDNAs.**

【180】**·May involve multiple tissues with high energy requirements-such as brain， retina， muscle， cochlea，etc.**

【182】**Diseases due to trinucleotide repeat expansions**

【183】**·Unstable expansion of trinucleotide repeats is the mechanism underlying disorders featuring anticipation， the tendency for subsequent generations to be affected at an earlier age and with increased severity.**

【184】**· The molecular mechanisms of disease are poorly understood as the triplet expansions are known to be located in coding sequences (Huntington disease)， non-coding sequences (Friedreich ataxia)， 5'-untranslated regions(fragile X syndrome)，and 3'-untranslated regions (myotonic dystrophy).**

【185】**·CAG repeat expansions that encode polyglutamines appear to result in protein misfolding， a recuring theme in many of these disorders.**

【186】**·DNA molecular diagnostic tests are available. However， estimating disease onset and severity within an individual is not accurately predicted by absolute repeat number. 【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【6】**·These features are mainly focused on longer periods of recommended observation relative to the patient’s age as outlined below.**

【7】**1 Coma and apnea must co-exist.**

【8】**2 Absence of brainstem function**

【9】2.1 Pupils unreactive to light (midposition or dilated).

【10】2.2 Absence of spontaneous eye movement， or in response to oculocephalic and oculovestibular testing.

【11】2.3 Absence of movement of bulbar musculature， including facial and oro-pharyngeal muscles (corneal，gag， cough，sucking， and rooting reflexes).

【12】2.4 Respiratory movements are absent with patient off the respirator.

【13】2.5 Apnea testing using standardized methods'can be performed.

【14】3 Absence of hypotension for age or hypothermia.

【175】**Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies**

【176】**·Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is nearly exclusively maternally inherited.**

【177】**· mtDNA is a closed， circular DNA molecule consisting of ~16，000nucleotides coding for 37 genes.**

【178】**· Every cell contains multiple mitochondria with multiple copies of DNA， a condition known as polyplasmy.**

【179】**·Mitochondrial diseases demonstrate a threshold effect， whereby disease onset and severity are a function of the balance between the proportion of mutant and wild-type mtDNAs.**

【180】**·May involve multiple tissues with high energy requirements-such as brain， retina， muscle， cochlea，etc.**

【182】**Diseases due to trinucleotide repeat expansions**

【183】**·Unstable expansion of trinucleotide repeats is the mechanism underlying disorders featuring anticipation， the tendency for subsequent generations to be affected at an earlier age and with increased severity.**

【184】**· The molecular mechanisms of disease are poorly understood as the triplet expansions are known to be located in coding sequences (Huntington disease)， non-coding sequences (Friedreich ataxia)， 5'-untranslated regions(fragile X syndrome)，and 3'-untranslated regions (myotonic dystrophy).**

【185】**·CAG repeat expansions that encode polyglutamines appear to result in protein misfolding， a recuring theme in many of these disorders.**

【186】**·DNA molecular diagnostic tests are available. However， estimating disease onset and severity within an individual is not accurately predicted by absolute repeat number. 【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【6】**·These features are mainly focused on longer periods of recommended observation relative to the patient’s age as outlined below.**

【183】**·Unstable expansion of trinucleotide repeats is the mechanism underlying disorders featuring anticipation， the tendency for subsequent generations to be affected at an earlier age and with increased severity.**

【184】**· The molecular mechanisms of disease are poorly understood as the triplet expansions are known to be located in coding sequences (Huntington disease)， non-coding sequences (Friedreich ataxia)， 5'-untranslated regions(fragile X syndrome)，and 3'-untranslated regions (myotonic dystrophy).**

【185】**·CAG repeat expansions that encode polyglutamines appear to result in protein misfolding， a recuring theme in many of these disorders.**

【186】**·DNA molecular diagnostic tests are available. However， estimating disease onset and severity within an individual is not accurately predicted by absolute repeat number. 【4】**Guidelines for the determination of brain death in children**

【5】**·The guidelines for determination of brain death in children are similar to adults， although they have some unique features， dealing specifically with the age group from full-term newborn to the 5-year-old.**

【176】**·Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is nearly exclusively maternally inherited.**

【14】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【16】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【17】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). In short， it is a T-cell lymphoma with a fulminant， fatal course. Multilobulated lymphocytes in the peripheral blood are markers of the disease. Those lymphocytes usually are of the T-helper/inducer immunophenotype， just as are those of mycosis fungoides.

【18】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. At that time， cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides may be the only ex-pressions of the disease； no internal ones may be discernible. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemialymphoma develops rapidly， and when patients see a physician， they not only have cutaneous manifestations， but lymphadenopa-thy， hepatosplenomegaly， and pulmonary involvement by the lymphoma-tous process. Hypercalcemia is frequent in patients with adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma.

【19】Histopathologic findings in plaques of mycosis fungoides and in pap-ules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma are startlingly similar， but they can be differentiated if heed is paid to the criteria set forth in this chapter.

【69】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【70】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【71】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. When all， or nearly all， of the findings listed at the outset of this chapter are found in a particular section of skin， a diagnosis of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles or follicular lym-phoma usually can be made readily. All too often， however， that good for-tune for a histopathologist is not the case， and， in those instances where a specific diagnosis is not apparent at first glance， an orderly method based upon a catechism must be applied diligently. That method utilizes architec-SPSS6tural pattern， as assessed at scanning magnification， as the surest route to differentiation betweenbenign and malignant neoplasms in general and between inflammatoryinfiltrates of lymphocytes in nodular and diffuse array， i.e.， pseudolymphomas， from authentic lymphomas in particular. The crucial attributes for a histopathologist to assess are where in the skin the infiltration of lymphocytes is most dense (“top-heavy”as in pseudolym-phomas or “bottom-heavy”as in lymphomas)， what shape does the infil-trate assume (wedge-shaped as is the case for some pseudolymphomas， or|删除0换行|not as in lymphomas)， how dense is the infiltrate (dense but not massive as in pseudolymphomas or massive sometimes as in lymphomas)， and how deep is the infiltrate (not simply into subcutaneous fat， as occurs in both pseudo- and lymphomas， but into skeletal muscles as happens only in lym-phomas as a rule). At higher magnifications， the decisive features that en-able distinction between the inflammatory and neoplastic process include“tingible bodies” (present commonly in germinal centers of pseudolympho-mas， but not in lymphomas)， striking pleomorphism of nuclei of lympho-cytes (pleomorphic in germinal centers of pseudolymphomas， but not out-side of those centers as they are in lymphomas)， and well-defined mantles of lymphocytes around germinal centers (prominent cuffs of lymphocytes are present in pseudolymphomas， but are ill-defined in lymphomas). These sets of distinguishing characteristics， when present in constellation， permit pseudolymphomas with lymphoid follicles to be discriminated from follicu-lar lymphomas in most instances.

【73】Similarities between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma exist clinically. Both the inflammatory and neoplastic processes are characterized clinicallv by painless papules， plaques， nodules， or tumors that vary in size and in color from red to violaceous. Both occur commonly on the head and neck. The presence of tumors of gigantic proportions favors a diagnosis of lym-phoma. As is true of malignant neoplasms in general， lymphomas continue to grow relentlessly； pseudolymphomas stop growing or even regress.

【74】Immunoperoxidase techniques may clarify the nature of an infiltrate of lymphocytes with associated follicles. The same principles that govern dif-ferentiation ofpseudolymphoma from lymphoma in sections stained by hematoxylin and eosin obtain equally for sections stained by immunoperox-idase techniques， to wit， a mixedpopulation favors pseudolymphoma， and a monomorphous population of llymphocytes favors lymphoma. Follicular lymphomas， being B-cell lymphomas， stain with B-cell markers in both lymphoid follicles and the interfollicular dermis and subcutaneous fat. Pseudolymphomnas tend to reproduce the normal architecture of a lymph node， i.e.， B-cells predominate in germinal centers， and T-cells predominate in the dermis between lymphoid follicles.

【75】Another difference between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma is re-vealed when immunoperoxidase techniques are used to detect expression of surface immunoglobulins. Lymphocytes of a pseudolymphoma express a mixture of lambda and kappa light chains. Lymphomas， on the contrary， express only one light chain or neither of them.

【76】Unfortunately， no matter what studies are performed， dense nodular and/or diffuse infiltrates of lymphocytes， with or without lymphoid follicles， may defy identification by current methods. In those situations， and if le-sions persist， additional biopsies should be taken over time and the patient followed carefully for signs of systemic manifestations of lymphoma.

【92】RITERIA for differentiation of xanthogranuloma from necrobiotic xanthogranuloma pertain to lesions of xanthogranuloma that are fully developed and of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma that are still evolving. These two conditions， at those different stages in their evolution， may be confused with one another because they have so many histopatho-logic features in common： predominance， or near predominance， of foam cells over other types of inflammatory cells； presence of Touton giant cells； mixed-cell infiltrates that contain lymphocytes， plasma cells， cosinophils， and histiocytes； extensive fibrosis； involvement of the subcutaneous fat； sparing of epidermis； and location， sometimes， on skin damaged badly by sunlight. It is important to identify these two conditions for what they are because they are so different biologically.

【93】Xanthogranuloma in skin affects children and adults differently. Histo-pathologically， however， the “juvenile" and “adult”types are indistinguish-able from one another. At an early stage， both are characterized by diffuse infiltrates of oval-shaped histiocytes in the upper part of the dermis. Mitotic figures may be present in those rapidly proliferating histiocytes marked sometimes by pleomorphic nuclei， and the lesion， at that stage， even may be misinterpreted as that of a carcinoma or sarcoma. In time， the cytoplasm of the histiocytes becomes increasingly foamy， Touton giant cells appear within the infiltrate， and the lesion is sprinkled with neutrophils， eosino-phils， lymphocytes， andplasma cells. Eventually，a cutaneousXan-thogranuloma undergoes regression by fibrosis.

【94】**Despite the fact that “juvenile”and “adult”expressions of cutaneous xanthogranuloma are indistinguishable from one another histopathologi-cally， they are different from one another clinically and biologically. Cutane-ous xanthogranuloma in adults presents itself usually as a solitary lesion and， nearly always， is not associated with xanthogranulomas in any other organ. In contrast， xanthogranulomas in children tend to be multiple and involve other organs such as the eyes， lungs， bones， kidneys， pericardium， colon， overies， and testes. Lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma have been associated at times with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromatoses. When an eye is affected by xanthogranuloma in a child， bleeding can occur and blind-ness may result. Xanthogranulomas in children and adults， because of their abundant lipid， appear clinically as yellow or yellow-orangc lesions. The clinical differential diagnosis of juvenile xanthogranuloma is nodular lesions of mastocytosis in children. Unlike the situation in adults， in whom a lesion of xanthogranuloma does not revert， the lesions in children involute.**

【95】**Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma usually affects persons who have passed the age of 50. The disease presents itself as papules and plaques， often on the periorbital areas of the face but also on the trunk and extremities， that tend to ulcerate. On the face， papules may become confluent and extend into an eye with resultant uveitis， iritis， and keratitis. On extremities， a lesion may resemble necrobiosis lipoidica closely. When a diagnosis of nec-robiotic xanthogranuloma has been established on histopathologic grounds， search must be undertaken for evidence of associated paraproteinemia with an IgG monoclonal gammopathy. In about one third of patients， a diagnosis of multiple mycloma is apparent from the outset. The disease progresses slowly to a fatal outcome.**

【96】**Histopathologically， as necrobiotic xanthogranuloma progresses be-yond the findings described at the outset of this chapter， the condition comes to resemble a caricature of necrobiosis lipoidica. When fully devel-oped， the process involves the entire dermis and much of the subcutaneous fat in the form of large zones of degeneration of collagen， within which there may be numerous cholesterol clefts and deposits of calcium. Zones of degenerated collagen often are surrounded by numerous foamy histiocytes that cnable necrobiotic xanthogranuloma to be differentiated from necrobi-osis lipoidica， in which there are none. Foam cells and calcification are consequences of necrosis of adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat. Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. Findings in fully developed lesions of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma are specific for that condition.**

【97】**In sum， at a stage in its evolution， necrobiotic xanthogranuloma may be misinterpreted as xanthogranuloma. The distinction is important be-cause the two conditions have very different prognoses. The criteria listed at the outset of this chapter should permit distinction between them.**

【69】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【70】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【71】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. When all， or nearly all， of the findings listed at the outset of this chapter are found in a particular section of skin， a diagnosis of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles or follicular lym-phoma usually can be made readily. All too often， however， that good for-tune for a histopathologist is not the case， and， in those instances where a specific diagnosis is not apparent at first glance， an orderly method based upon a catechism must be applied diligently. That method utilizes architec-SPSS6tural pattern， as assessed at scanning magnification， as the surest route to differentiation betweenbenign and malignant neoplasms in general and between inflammatoryinfiltrates of lymphocytes in nodular and diffuse array， i.e.， pseudolymphomas， from authentic lymphomas in particular. The crucial attributes for a histopathologist to assess are where in the skin the infiltration of lymphocytes is most dense (“top-heavy”as in pseudolym-phomas or “bottom-heavy”as in lymphomas)， what shape does the infil-trate assume (wedge-shaped as is the case for some pseudolymphomas， or|删除0换行|not as in lymphomas)， how dense is the infiltrate (dense but not massive as in pseudolymphomas or massive sometimes as in lymphomas)， and how deep is the infiltrate (not simply into subcutaneous fat， as occurs in both pseudo- and lymphomas， but into skeletal muscles as happens only in lym-phomas as a rule). At higher magnifications， the decisive features that en-able distinction between the inflammatory and neoplastic process include“tingible bodies” (present commonly in germinal centers of pseudolympho-mas， but not in lymphomas)， striking pleomorphism of nuclei of lympho-cytes (pleomorphic in germinal centers of pseudolymphomas， but not out-side of those centers as they are in lymphomas)， and well-defined mantles of lymphocytes around germinal centers (prominent cuffs of lymphocytes are present in pseudolymphomas， but are ill-defined in lymphomas). These sets of distinguishing characteristics， when present in constellation， permit pseudolymphomas with lymphoid follicles to be discriminated from follicu-lar lymphomas in most instances.

【73】Similarities between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma exist clinically. Both the inflammatory and neoplastic processes are characterized clinicallv by painless papules， plaques， nodules， or tumors that vary in size and in color from red to violaceous. Both occur commonly on the head and neck. The presence of tumors of gigantic proportions favors a diagnosis of lym-phoma. As is true of malignant neoplasms in general， lymphomas continue to grow relentlessly； pseudolymphomas stop growing or even regress.

【74】Immunoperoxidase techniques may clarify the nature of an infiltrate of lymphocytes with associated follicles. The same principles that govern dif-ferentiation ofpseudolymphoma from lymphoma in sections stained by hematoxylin and eosin obtain equally for sections stained by immunoperox-idase techniques， to wit， a mixedpopulation favors pseudolymphoma， and a monomorphous population of llymphocytes favors lymphoma. Follicular lymphomas， being B-cell lymphomas， stain with B-cell markers in both lymphoid follicles and the interfollicular dermis and subcutaneous fat. Pseudolymphomnas tend to reproduce the normal architecture of a lymph node， i.e.， B-cells predominate in germinal centers， and T-cells predominate in the dermis between lymphoid follicles.

【75】Another difference between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma is re-vealed when immunoperoxidase techniques are used to detect expression of surface immunoglobulins. Lymphocytes of a pseudolymphoma express a mixture of lambda and kappa light chains. Lymphomas， on the contrary， express only one light chain or neither of them.

【76】Unfortunately， no matter what studies are performed， dense nodular and/or diffuse infiltrates of lymphocytes， with or without lymphoid follicles， may defy identification by current methods. In those situations， and if le-sions persist， additional biopsies should be taken over time and the patient followed carefully for signs of systemic manifestations of lymphoma.

【92】RITERIA for differentiation of xanthogranuloma from necrobiotic xanthogranuloma pertain to lesions of xanthogranuloma that are fully developed and of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma that are still evolving. These two conditions， at those different stages in their evolution， may be confused with one another because they have so many histopatho-logic features in common： predominance， or near predominance， of foam cells over other types of inflammatory cells； presence of Touton giant cells； mixed-cell infiltrates that contain lymphocytes， plasma cells， cosinophils， and histiocytes； extensive fibrosis； involvement of the subcutaneous fat； sparing of epidermis； and location， sometimes， on skin damaged badly by sunlight. It is important to identify these two conditions for what they are because they are so different biologically.

【93】Xanthogranuloma in skin affects children and adults differently. Histo-pathologically， however， the “juvenile" and “adult”types are indistinguish-able from one another. At an early stage， both are characterized by diffuse infiltrates of oval-shaped histiocytes in the upper part of the dermis. Mitotic figures may be present in those rapidly proliferating histiocytes marked sometimes by pleomorphic nuclei， and the lesion， at that stage， even may be misinterpreted as that of a carcinoma or sarcoma. In time， the cytoplasm of the histiocytes becomes increasingly foamy， Touton giant cells appear within the infiltrate， and the lesion is sprinkled with neutrophils， eosino-phils， lymphocytes， andplasma cells. Eventually，a cutaneousXan-thogranuloma undergoes regression by fibrosis.

【94】**Despite the fact that “juvenile”and “adult”expressions of cutaneous xanthogranuloma are indistinguishable from one another histopathologi-cally， they are different from one another clinically and biologically. Cutane-ous xanthogranuloma in adults presents itself usually as a solitary lesion and， nearly always， is not associated with xanthogranulomas in any other organ. In contrast， xanthogranulomas in children tend to be multiple and involve other organs such as the eyes， lungs， bones， kidneys， pericardium， colon， overies， and testes. Lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma have been associated at times with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromatoses. When an eye is affected by xanthogranuloma in a child， bleeding can occur and blind-ness may result. Xanthogranulomas in children and adults， because of their abundant lipid， appear clinically as yellow or yellow-orangc lesions. The clinical differential diagnosis of juvenile xanthogranuloma is nodular lesions of mastocytosis in children. Unlike the situation in adults， in whom a lesion of xanthogranuloma does not revert， the lesions in children involute.**

【95】**Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma usually affects persons who have passed the age of 50. The disease presents itself as papules and plaques， often on the periorbital areas of the face but also on the trunk and extremities， that tend to ulcerate. On the face， papules may become confluent and extend into an eye with resultant uveitis， iritis， and keratitis. On extremities， a lesion may resemble necrobiosis lipoidica closely. When a diagnosis of nec-robiotic xanthogranuloma has been established on histopathologic grounds， search must be undertaken for evidence of associated paraproteinemia with an IgG monoclonal gammopathy. In about one third of patients， a diagnosis of multiple mycloma is apparent from the outset. The disease progresses slowly to a fatal outcome.**

【96】**Histopathologically， as necrobiotic xanthogranuloma progresses be-yond the findings described at the outset of this chapter， the condition comes to resemble a caricature of necrobiosis lipoidica. When fully devel-oped， the process involves the entire dermis and much of the subcutaneous fat in the form of large zones of degeneration of collagen， within which there may be numerous cholesterol clefts and deposits of calcium. Zones of degenerated collagen often are surrounded by numerous foamy histiocytes that cnable necrobiotic xanthogranuloma to be differentiated from necrobi-osis lipoidica， in which there are none. Foam cells and calcification are consequences of necrosis of adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat. Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. Findings in fully developed lesions of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma are specific for that condition.**

【97】**In sum， at a stage in its evolution， necrobiotic xanthogranuloma may be misinterpreted as xanthogranuloma. The distinction is important be-cause the two conditions have very different prognoses. The criteria listed at the outset of this chapter should permit distinction between them.**

【14】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【16】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【17】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). 【18】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. 【14】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【16】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【17】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). In short， it is a T-cell lymphoma with a fulminant， fatal course. Multilobulated lymphocytes in the peripheral blood are markers of the disease. Those lymphocytes usually are of the T-helper/inducer immunophenotype， just as are those of mycosis fungoides.

【18】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. At that time， cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides may be the only ex-pressions of the disease； no internal ones may be discernible. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemialymphoma develops rapidly， and when patients see a physician， they not only have cutaneous manifestations， but lymphadenopa-thy， hepatosplenomegaly， and pulmonary involvement by the lymphoma-tous process. Hypercalcemia is frequent in patients with adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma.

【19】Histopathologic findings in plaques of mycosis fungoides and in pap-ules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma are startlingly similar， but they can be differentiated if heed is paid to the criteria set forth in this chapter.

【69】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【70】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【71】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. When all， or nearly all， of the findings listed at the outset of this chapter are found in a particular section of skin， a diagnosis of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles or follicular lym-phoma usually can be made readily. All too often， however， that good for-tune for a histopathologist is not the case， and， in those instances where a specific diagnosis is not apparent at first glance， an orderly method based upon a catechism must be applied diligently. That method utilizes architec-SPSS6tural pattern， as assessed at scanning magnification， as the surest route to differentiation betweenbenign and malignant neoplasms in general and between inflammatoryinfiltrates of lymphocytes in nodular and diffuse array， i.e.， pseudolymphomas， from authentic lymphomas in particular. The crucial attributes for a histopathologist to assess are where in the skin the infiltration of lymphocytes is most dense (“top-heavy”as in pseudolym-phomas or “bottom-heavy”as in lymphomas)， what shape does the infil-trate assume (wedge-shaped as is the case for some pseudolymphomas， or|删除0换行|not as in lymphomas)， how dense is the infiltrate (dense but not massive as in pseudolymphomas or massive sometimes as in lymphomas)， and how deep is the infiltrate (not simply into subcutaneous fat， as occurs in both pseudo- and lymphomas， but into skeletal muscles as happens only in lym-phomas as a rule). At higher magnifications， the decisive features that en-able distinction between the inflammatory and neoplastic process include“tingible bodies” (present commonly in germinal centers of pseudolympho-mas， but not in lymphomas)， striking pleomorphism of nuclei of lympho-cytes (pleomorphic in germinal centers of pseudolymphomas， but not out-side of those centers as they are in lymphomas)， and well-defined mantles of lymphocytes around germinal centers (prominent cuffs of lymphocytes are present in pseudolymphomas， but are ill-defined in lymphomas). These sets of distinguishing characteristics， when present in constellation， permit pseudolymphomas with lymphoid follicles to be discriminated from follicu-lar lymphomas in most instances.

【73】Similarities between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma exist clinically. Both the inflammatory and neoplastic processes are characterized clinicallv by painless papules， plaques， nodules， or tumors that vary in size and in color from red to violaceous. Both occur commonly on the head and neck. The presence of tumors of gigantic proportions favors a diagnosis of lym-phoma. As is true of malignant neoplasms in general， lymphomas continue to grow relentlessly； pseudolymphomas stop growing or even regress.

【74】Immunoperoxidase techniques may clarify the nature of an infiltrate of lymphocytes with associated follicles. The same principles that govern dif-ferentiation ofpseudolymphoma from lymphoma in sections stained by hematoxylin and eosin obtain equally for sections stained by immunoperox-idase techniques， to wit， a mixedpopulation favors pseudolymphoma， and a monomorphous population of llymphocytes favors lymphoma. Follicular lymphomas， being B-cell lymphomas， stain with B-cell markers in both lymphoid follicles and the interfollicular dermis and subcutaneous fat. Pseudolymphomnas tend to reproduce the normal architecture of a lymph node， i.e.， B-cells predominate in germinal centers， and T-cells predominate in the dermis between lymphoid follicles.

【75】Another difference between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma is re-vealed when immunoperoxidase techniques are used to detect expression of surface immunoglobulins. Lymphocytes of a pseudolymphoma express a mixture of lambda and kappa light chains. Lymphomas， on the contrary， express only one light chain or neither of them.

【76】Unfortunately， no matter what studies are performed， dense nodular and/or diffuse infiltrates of lymphocytes， with or without lymphoid follicles， may defy identification by current methods. In those situations， and if le-sions persist， additional biopsies should be taken over time and the patient followed carefully for signs of systemic manifestations of lymphoma.

【92】RITERIA for differentiation of xanthogranuloma from necrobiotic xanthogranuloma pertain to lesions of xanthogranuloma that are fully developed and of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma that are still evolving. These two conditions， at those different stages in their evolution， may be confused with one another because they have so many histopatho-logic features in common： predominance， or near predominance， of foam cells over other types of inflammatory cells； presence of Touton giant cells； mixed-cell infiltrates that contain lymphocytes， plasma cells， cosinophils， and histiocytes； extensive fibrosis； involvement of the subcutaneous fat； sparing of epidermis； and location， sometimes， on skin damaged badly by sunlight. It is important to identify these two conditions for what they are because they are so different biologically.

【93】Xanthogranuloma in skin affects children and adults differently. Histo-pathologically， however， the “juvenile" and “adult”types are indistinguish-able from one another. At an early stage， both are characterized by diffuse infiltrates of oval-shaped histiocytes in the upper part of the dermis. Mitotic figures may be present in those rapidly proliferating histiocytes marked sometimes by pleomorphic nuclei， and the lesion， at that stage， even may be misinterpreted as that of a carcinoma or sarcoma. In time， the cytoplasm of the histiocytes becomes increasingly foamy， Touton giant cells appear within the infiltrate， and the lesion is sprinkled with neutrophils， eosino-phils， lymphocytes， andplasma cells. Eventually，a cutaneousXan-thogranuloma undergoes regression by fibrosis.

【94】**Despite the fact that “juvenile”and “adult”expressions of cutaneous xanthogranuloma are indistinguishable from one another histopathologi-cally， they are different from one another clinically and biologically. Cutane-ous xanthogranuloma in adults presents itself usually as a solitary lesion and， nearly always， is not associated with xanthogranulomas in any other organ. In contrast， xanthogranulomas in children tend to be multiple and involve other organs such as the eyes， lungs， bones， kidneys， pericardium， colon， overies， and testes. Lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma have been associated at times with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromatoses. When an eye is affected by xanthogranuloma in a child， bleeding can occur and blind-ness may result. Xanthogranulomas in children and adults， because of their abundant lipid， appear clinically as yellow or yellow-orangc lesions. The clinical differential diagnosis of juvenile xanthogranuloma is nodular lesions of mastocytosis in children. Unlike the situation in adults， in whom a lesion of xanthogranuloma does not revert， the lesions in children involute.**

【95】**Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma usually affects persons who have passed the age of 50. The disease presents itself as papules and plaques， often on the periorbital areas of the face but also on the trunk and extremities， that tend to ulcerate. On the face， papules may become confluent and extend into an eye with resultant uveitis， iritis， and keratitis. On extremities， a lesion may resemble necrobiosis lipoidica closely. When a diagnosis of nec-robiotic xanthogranuloma has been established on histopathologic grounds， search must be undertaken for evidence of associated paraproteinemia with an IgG monoclonal gammopathy. In about one third of patients， a diagnosis of multiple mycloma is apparent from the outset. The disease progresses slowly to a fatal outcome.**

【96】**Histopathologically， as necrobiotic xanthogranuloma progresses be-yond the findings described at the outset of this chapter， the condition comes to resemble a caricature of necrobiosis lipoidica. When fully devel-oped， the process involves the entire dermis and much of the subcutaneous fat in the form of large zones of degeneration of collagen， within which there may be numerous cholesterol clefts and deposits of calcium. Zones of degenerated collagen often are surrounded by numerous foamy histiocytes that cnable necrobiotic xanthogranuloma to be differentiated from necrobi-osis lipoidica， in which there are none. Foam cells and calcification are consequences of necrosis of adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat. Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. Findings in fully developed lesions of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma are specific for that condition.**

【97】**In sum， at a stage in its evolution， necrobiotic xanthogranuloma may be misinterpreted as xanthogranuloma. The distinction is important be-cause the two conditions have very different prognoses. The criteria listed at the outset of this chapter should permit distinction between them.**

【69】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【70】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【71】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. 【73】Similarities between pseudolymphoma and lymphoma exist clinically. Both the inflammatory and neoplastic processes are characterized clinicallv by painless papules， plaques， nodules， or tumors that vary in size and in color from red to violaceous. Both occur commonly on the head and neck. The presence of tumors of gigantic proportions favors a diagnosis of lym-phoma. 【92】RITERIA for differentiation of xanthogranuloma from necrobiotic xanthogranuloma pertain to lesions of xanthogranuloma that are fully developed and of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma that are still evolving. These two conditions， at those different stages in their evolution， may be confused with one another because they have so many histopatho-logic features in common： predominance， or near predominance， of foam cells over other types of inflammatory cells； presence of Touton giant cells； mixed-cell infiltrates that contain lymphocytes， plasma cells， cosinophils， and histiocytes； extensive fibrosis； involvement of the subcutaneous fat； sparing of epidermis； and location， sometimes， on skin damaged badly by sunlight. It is important to identify these two conditions for what they are because they are so different biologically.

【93】Xanthogranuloma in skin affects children and adults differently. Histo-pathologically， however， the “juvenile" and “adult”types are indistinguish-able from one another. At an early stage， both are characterized by diffuse infiltrates of oval-shaped histiocytes in the upper part of the dermis. Mitotic figures may be present in those rapidly proliferating histiocytes marked sometimes by pleomorphic nuclei， and the lesion， at that stage， even may be misinterpreted as that of a carcinoma or sarcoma. In time， the cytoplasm of the histiocytes becomes increasingly foamy， Touton giant cells appear within the infiltrate， and the lesion is sprinkled with neutrophils， eosino-phils， lymphocytes， andplasma cells. Eventually，a cutaneousXan-thogranuloma undergoes regression by fibrosis.

【94】**Despite the fact that “juvenile”and “adult”expressions of cutaneous xanthogranuloma are indistinguishable from one another histopathologi-cally， they are different from one another clinically and biologically. Cutane-ous xanthogranuloma in adults presents itself usually as a solitary lesion and， nearly always， is not associated with xanthogranulomas in any other organ. In contrast， xanthogranulomas in children tend to be multiple and involve other organs such as the eyes， lungs， bones， kidneys， pericardium， colon， overies， and testes. Lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma have been associated at times with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromatoses. When an eye is affected by xanthogranuloma in a child， bleeding can occur and blind-ness may result. Xanthogranulomas in children and adults， because of their abundant lipid， appear clinically as yellow or yellow-orangc lesions. The clinical differential diagnosis of juvenile xanthogranuloma is nodular lesions of mastocytosis in children. Unlike the situation in adults， in whom a lesion of xanthogranuloma does not revert， the lesions in children involute.**

【95】**Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma usually affects persons who have passed the age of 50. The disease presents itself as papules and plaques， often on the periorbital areas of the face but also on the trunk and extremities， that tend to ulcerate. On the face， papules may become confluent and extend into an eye with resultant uveitis， iritis， and keratitis. On extremities， a lesion may resemble necrobiosis lipoidica closely. When a diagnosis of nec-robiotic xanthogranuloma has been established on histopathologic grounds， search must be undertaken for evidence of associated paraproteinemia with an IgG monoclonal gammopathy. In about one third of patients， a diagnosis of multiple mycloma is apparent from the outset. The disease progresses slowly to a fatal outcome.**

【96】**Histopathologically， as necrobiotic xanthogranuloma progresses be-yond the findings described at the outset of this chapter， the condition comes to resemble a caricature of necrobiosis lipoidica. When fully devel-oped， the process involves the entire dermis and much of the subcutaneous fat in the form of large zones of degeneration of collagen， within which there may be numerous cholesterol clefts and deposits of calcium. Zones of degenerated collagen often are surrounded by numerous foamy histiocytes that cnable necrobiotic xanthogranuloma to be differentiated from necrobi-osis lipoidica， in which there are none. Foam cells and calcification are consequences of necrosis of adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat. Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. Findings in fully developed lesions of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma are specific for that condition.**

【97】**In sum， at a stage in its evolution， necrobiotic xanthogranuloma may be misinterpreted as xanthogranuloma. The distinction is important be-cause the two conditions have very different prognoses. The criteria listed at the outset of this chapter should permit distinction between them.**

【14】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【16】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【17】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). In short， it is a T-cell lymphoma with a fulminant， fatal course. Multilobulated lymphocytes in the peripheral blood are markers of the disease. Those lymphocytes usually are of the T-helper/inducer immunophenotype， just as are those of mycosis fungoides.

【18】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. At that time， cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides may be the only ex-pressions of the disease； no internal ones may be discernible. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemialymphoma develops rapidly， and when patients see a physician， they not only have cutaneous manifestations， but lymphadenopa-thy， hepatosplenomegaly， and pulmonary involvement by the lymphoma-tous process. Hypercalcemia is frequent in patients with adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma.

【19】Histopathologic findings in plaques of mycosis fungoides and in pap-ules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma are startlingly similar， but they can be differentiated if heed is paid to the criteria set forth in this chapter.

Lympho-plasmocytic infiltrates， like those in necrobiosis lipoidica， are present throughout the dermis and the subcutaneous fat. 【14】LAQUES of mycosis fungoides and1papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have many features in common， among them the presence of atypical lymphocytes， epidermotropism of lympho-cytes， atypical lymphocytes arranged both as solitary units and in collections within the epidermis， lymphocytes aligned in the basal layer of the epider-mis sometimes， lymphocytes in the epidermis larger than some of them within the dermis， a psoriasiform or psoriasiform lichenoid pattern， an infiltrate of lymphocytes that is mostly superficial， lymphocytes sometimes situated in the upper reaches of the epidermis including the cornified layer， intraepidermal collections of lymphocytes that vary in size， epithelial struc-tures of adnexa permeated by lymphocytes sometimes， wiry bundles of col-lagen in haphazard array in the papillary dermis at times， and coarse bun-dles of collagen in vertical streaks in a thickened papillary dermis (lichen simplex chronicus). In some specimens， atypical lymphocytes in both dis-eases may be confined wholly to the dermis with no evidence of epider-motropism.

Mycosis fungoides in the plaque stage can be differentiated histopatho-logically from adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in the papular stage by both architectural and cytologic features. Cytologically， lymphocytes in mycosis fungoides have less cytoplasm， are relatively monomorphous， are more cer-ebriform (and more of them are cerebriform)， and are not associated with abundant nuclear “dust.” The latter finding reflects the fact that lympho-cytes in mycosis fungoides do not undergo necrosis readily. Furthermore， eosinophils are present commonly within plaques of mycosis fungoides， but not in papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Although both plaques of mycosis fungoides and papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma may be associated with prominent collections of atypical lymphocytes within the epidermis， large collections of them are much more common in leukemia/lymphoma (where there are many more of them). Even when collections of atypical lymphocytes form within the epidermis of plaques of mycosis fun-goides， the collections tend to be small and usually seem insignificant in comparison with the atypical lymphocytes that pepper the epidermis as solitary units. In adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma， collections of atypical lymphocytes tend to predominate over atypical lymphocytes arranged as solitary units within the epidermis. Because plaques of mycosis fungoides are long-standing by the time that they come to be biopsied， in contrast to papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma that are relatively short-lived at the time they are sampled by biopsy， differences in quantity of wiry bundles of collagen in the thickened papillary dermis are to be expected. In mycosis|删除0换行|fungoides， extensive repiacement of the normal papillary dermis by wiry collagen bundles in haphazard array is common， whereas those alterations， when they are present at all in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma，are subtle. Another sign of chronicity in plaques of mycosis fungoides is absence of edema from the papillary dermis； edema in papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma indicates acutcness of thatprocess.

【16】Just as patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides share many histo-oathologic features with patients who havepapules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma， so， too， it is for clinical lesions of those diseases. Both diseases may be constituted of macules， papules， patches， plaques， nodules， tumors， and ulcerated tumors. Patients with plaques of mycosis fungoides， however， may exhibit discrete plaques only， and not a potpourri of other cutaneous lesions. In contrast， patients with papules of adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma almost always have numerous nodules， too. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually favor the buttocks and the trunk. Papules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma have a predilection for the extremities， which may become markedly edematous. Plaques of mycosis fungoides usually do not ulcerate， whereasSpapules and nodules of adult T-cellleukemia/lymphoma may ulcerate and be covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Whereas patches and plaques tend to predominate in mycosis fungoides， papules usually predominate in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Papules are un-common in mycosis fungoides.

【17】The cause of mycosis fungoides is not known. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma has been demonstrated to be a lympho-proliferative disorder induced by a type C retrovirus (HTLV-3). In short， it is a T-cell lymphoma with a fulminant， fatal course. Multilobulated lymphocytes in the peripheral blood are markers of the disease. Those lymphocytes usually are of the T-helper/inducer immunophenotype， just as are those of mycosis fungoides.

【18】Plaques of mycosis fungoides signify that the disease has been present in the skin for many years before a patient has come to a physician. At that time， cutaneous manifestations of mycosis fungoides may be the only ex-pressions of the disease； no internal ones may be discernible. In contrast， adult T-cell leukemialymphoma develops rapidly， and when patients see a physician， they not only have cutaneous manifestations， but lymphadenopa-thy， hepatosplenomegaly， and pulmonary involvement by the lymphoma-tous process. Hypercalcemia is frequent in patients with adult T-cell leu-kemia/lymphoma.

【19】Histopathologic findings in plaques of mycosis fungoides and in pap-ules of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma are startlingly similar， but they can be differentiated if heed is paid to the criteria set forth in this chapter.

【69】Amajor trial for histopathologists may be posed by differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicu-lar lymphoma. The reasons are obvious. Even pseudolymphomas devoid of lymphoid follicles may confound histopathologists who seek to differentiate them from malignant lymphomas. That difficulty is compounded when lymphoid follicles， reputed to be a sign of pseudolymphomas， are present in authentic lymphomas. The follicular lymphoma under discussion in this chapter is a B-cell lymphoma.

【70】At the outset， a clear distinction must be made between primary and secondary lymphoid follicles. The attributes of those two structures are based upon findings in normal lymph nodes. Primary follicles are those in which lymphocytes have monomorphous nuclei， and secondary follicles are those that contain germinal centers. In this discussion of criteria for histo-pathologic differentiation of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles from follicular lymphoma， secondary follicles alone are germane.

【71】Common to both pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles and follicu-lar lymphoma are dense nodular or diffuse predominantly lymphocytic in-filtrates within the dermis and， often， within the subcutaneous fat， lymph-oid follicleswithin the dermis andsometimes the subcutaneousfat， lymphocytes in mitosis， at least two populations of lymphocytes， na small and large ones， and absence of epidermal involvement.

It is well known to dermatopathologists that， in attempting to distin-guish infiltrates of lymphocytes in inflammatory diseases that simulate lym-phomas from those in true lymphomas， criteria cmployed for that purpose are flawed， sometimes seriously. When all， or nearly all， of the findings listed at the outset of this chapter are found in a particular section of skin， a diagnosis of pseudolymphoma with lymphoid follicles or follicular lym-phoma usually can be made readily.
